subtype: Approach: sees which tasks must finish before others can start [Thinking]
passage: The district science exhibition was ten days away, and Raghav and Hrithik had decided on a clay model of a village water filter. At the back of the kasba school's lab, Raghav drew boxes on the blackboard and argued with himself out loud. "We want to paint it blue and brown. But wet clay won't hold paint. The model needs two full days to dry. So shaping is first, no matter what." He drew an arrow. "Our write-up depends on what the muddy-water test shows. We can't write what we haven't tested." Another arrow. "So: shape, then test while it dries, then paint, then report." Hrithik squinted. "Why not start the report now? It's easy marks." "Because we'd just rewrite it." They began kneading clay that afternoon.

qa.q: How long does the clay model need to dry?
qa.a: Two full days to dry.

qa.q: How can you tell Raghav felt sure about the order?
qa.a: He drew arrows and answered Hrithik firmly, so he seemed confident that shaping and testing had to come before painting and the report.

qa.q: What else could the pair do while the clay dries?
qa.a: They could do the muddy-water test and prepare the report's headings and diagrams, which don't depend on the results.

qa.q: How does Hrithik see Raghav's plan at first?
qa.a: He's doubtful and impatient, wanting the easy report marks first, until Raghav explains they'd only have to rewrite it.

grounding: A student planning an exhibition sees the model must dry before painting and the report needs results, so those come first.

subtype: Approach: sees which tasks must finish before others can start [Thinking]
passage: In a classroom in Valencia, Javier and Amara had a week before the school science fair. Their project: a papier-mâché volcano to show how acids and bases react. Amara wanted to start with the poster and write-up. Javier took the whiteboard marker. "Hang on. Let's see what has to happen first." He wrote: build, dry, paint, test, write. "The papier-mâché needs three nights to dry. We can't paint it wet, it'll just slide off. And the write-up is about what happened when we tested different amounts of vinegar. We don't know that yet." Amara folded her arms. "So I do nothing?" "No, you run the vinegar tests in cups while the volcano dries. Then we both write." She considered it and nodded.

qa.q: How many nights does the papier-mâché need to dry?
qa.a: Three nights to dry.

qa.q: What was Amara feeling when she asked, 'So I do nothing?'
qa.a: She felt left out and a little annoyed, worried the plan gave her no part while the volcano dried.

qa.q: What would you advise the pair if the volcano is still damp on day four?
qa.a: Keep testing and drafting the method part of the write-up, and paint only once it's fully dry.

qa.q: What would change if they had started with the poster and write-up, as Amara first wanted?
qa.a: They would likely have to redo the write-up after testing and might paint a damp volcano, wasting part of their one week.

grounding: A student sees that the model must dry before it is painted and the report needs test results, so those tasks come first.

subtype: Approach: maps the longest chain of dependent tasks to see the minimum time [Thinking]
passage: In the small college library in Karad, Uday and Siddharth had six weeks for their survey project on how farmers use weather messages. Siddharth wanted to design the report cover first. Uday unrolled a sheet of chart paper. "Let's list everything and see what depends on what." He talked it through as he drew. "Visiting forty farmers takes three weeks, because the bus to the villages only runs twice a day. We can't analyse until the data is in: one week. The report needs the analysis: one more week. That's five weeks just for that line. Everything else, the cover, the slides, the thank-you letters, can happen alongside." He underlined the long line in red. "If the village visits slip even a week, we're finished." Siddharth stopped doodling. "Then we book the first bus tomorrow."

qa.q: How many farmers did the team plan to visit?
qa.a: Forty farmers.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel when Uday underlined the long line in red?
qa.a: Siddharth seemed to feel a jolt of worry, stopping his doodling once he saw how little slack there was.

qa.q: What could the team do to protect the longest chain?
qa.a: Start village visits at once and split the farmers between them, so a missed bus doesn't delay analysis and the report.

qa.q: How might the farmers see the students' visits?
qa.a: Some farmers might welcome being asked about the weather messages, as long as the students come on time and don't rush them.

grounding: A student team maps data collection, analysis and report as the longest chain, so any delay there delays everything.

subtype: Approach: maps the longest chain of dependent tasks to see the minimum time [Thinking]
passage: In a seminar room at the university in Cape Town, Ada and Lindiwe had a month for their river water project. Ada stuck sticky notes on the wall: collect samples, lab tests, analysis, write-up, poster, presentation. "Now arrows," Lindiwe said. They drew them together. Ada thought aloud. "Samples take a week, because we need three different days after rain. Lab tests need the samples, that's another week. Analysis needs the tests, four days. Write-up needs the analysis." She stepped back. "That chain is almost the whole month. The poster and slides can float." Lindiwe tapped the first note. "So if it doesn't rain this week, we're already late." Ada frowned. "Then we ask the supervisor about a backup site with steady flow."

qa.q: How long does sample collection take?
qa.a: A week, because they need three different days after rain.

qa.q: What was Ada feeling when she stepped back from the wall?
qa.a: Ada felt a flash of alarm, seeing the chain filled almost the whole month.

qa.q: What else could Ada and Lindiwe do if the rain doesn't come?
qa.a: Use the backup site with steady flow, after checking with the supervisor, so the long chain can start on time.

qa.q: What is it like for the supervisor to be asked about a backup site early?
qa.a: The supervisor can help while there's still time, instead of hearing about a crisis at the deadline.

grounding: A student team finds that sampling, testing, analysis and write-up form the longest chain, so any delay there delays everything.

subtype: Approach: starts long-lead items early and does small tasks in the gaps [Action]
passage: You asked what my first rule is. I'm Noor, I've planned weddings for three years, and my first rule is: order the cards before anything else. Take Avni's wedding last winter. Her cards had gold foil and were printed in two languages. The press needed two full weeks. So on the very first day, before the caterer, before the flowers, before the venue decoration, I sent the approved design to the press. Then, while those two weeks ticked by, I made my calls. Monday, the caterer. Tuesday, the tent house. Wednesday, the photographer and the mehendi artist. Friday, the band. By the time the cards came back, every vendor had confirmed. Avni's mother said it was the calmest wedding in their family.

qa.q: How long did the press need for the cards?
qa.a: Two full weeks.

qa.q: How did Avni's mother seem to feel about the wedding?
qa.a: She seemed relieved and grateful, calling it the calmest wedding in their family.

qa.q: Which approach made Noor's plan work?
qa.a: Starting the longest job, the cards, on day one, then using the waiting time to confirm vendors, so nothing waited on anything else.

qa.q: How might Avni see Noor's method?
qa.a: Avni probably felt calmer, knowing the cards were being printed and every vendor confirmed well before the wedding 😊

grounding: A wedding planner orders the printed cards first because they take two weeks and fills the waiting time with vendor calls.

subtype: Approach: starts long-lead items early and does small tasks in the gaps [Action]
passage: My name's Shreya. I started as Ira's assistant at the wedding firm this spring, and on my first day I watched her work. The client wanted hand-lettered Urdu cards, and the calligrapher said sixteen days. Ira didn't open the decor folder or the menu. She called the calligrapher first and sent the approved text before lunch. Then she turned to me. "Now we have sixteen days of waiting. Don't waste them." She gave me a list: confirm the mehendi artist, call three tent houses for quotes, book the sound system. Every time the calligrapher sent an update, Ira checked it in five minutes and went back to the list. I can't tell what she was feeling, but she never looked hurried. The cards came on day fifteen.

qa.q: How many days did the calligrapher say the cards would take?
qa.a: Sixteen days.

qa.q: What does Ira's never looking hurried suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt calm and in control, because the slowest task had started first.

qa.q: What could Shreya learn to do on her own next time?
qa.a: Ask on day one which item takes longest, start that, and plan other tasks to fill the waiting time.

qa.q: How might the client feel when the cards arrive a day early?
qa.a: The client would likely feel relieved and reassured that the wedding is in good hands.

grounding: An observer watches a wedding planner order the slow printed cards first and fill the waiting time with vendor calls.

subtype: Approach: focuses on the visible tasks and ignores a hidden dependency [Pitfall]
passage: Nikita, sit, I'll tell you about the worst launch of my life. I was twenty-five, at my first startup, making a food-ordering app for small towns. We spent every day making the screens beautiful. Colours, icons, little animations when you tapped. We were so proud. Two weeks before launch, someone asked, "Has the payment gateway approved us?" Silence. Nobody had even applied. Nobody had written it on any list. The approval took a month. We sat with a lovely app that couldn't take a single rupee. Our launch moved by five weeks, and the local restaurants we'd signed up went cold on us. That's why Kalyani Aunty asks you so many boring questions about paperwork. It's what hides that hurts you.

qa.q: How long did the payment approval take?
qa.a: The approval took a month.

qa.q: What was the team feeling when someone asked about the payment gateway?
qa.a: They were shocked and embarrassed; the silence showed nobody had even thought of applying.

qa.q: At what point in the story could the team have avoided the slip?
qa.a: At the planning stage, if someone had listed every outside approval and started the slow one first, before polishing the screens.

qa.q: How did the local restaurants see the delay?
qa.a: They went cold on the app, probably feeling let down and unsure it would ever launch.

grounding: An elder recalls a team polishing app screens while forgetting a month-long payment approval, so the launch slipped.

subtype: Approach: focuses on the visible tasks and ignores a hidden dependency [Pitfall]
passage: The festival season was six weeks away, and Anirban's team had promised to launch their ticket-booking app before it. With only three developers and one designer, they worked late every night. Anirban kept the task board full of visible things: home screen, seat map, colour themes, a smooth scrolling list. Anand, the designer, redid the icons twice. In week four, Anirban opened an email from the bank. "Your payment gateway application will be reviewed in 30 working days." His stomach dropped. Nobody had put it on the board; each of them had assumed someone else had applied. The launch moved past the festival. Anand slumped in his chair. "All those icons," he said, "and nobody can pay for a ticket."

qa.q: How long did the bank say the review would take?
qa.a: 30 working days.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he read the bank's email?
qa.a: He felt a sinking dread; his stomach dropped when he saw the launch would miss the festival.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Each person assumed someone else had applied; listing every outside approval on the board, with an owner, would catch it early.

qa.q: How does Anand see the outcome?
qa.a: Anand feels deflated and frustrated that the icons he redid twice can't help, because nobody can pay for a ticket.

grounding: A team polishes visible app screens but misses the month-long payment approval nobody listed, and the launch slips.

subtype: Approach: redraws the path when a delay appears and shifts resources [Revision]
passage: I'm Leela, one of the four developers in Rafiq's team, and I watched how he handled the week our launch nearly fell apart. On Tuesday, the bank said our payment approval would take ten more days than promised. Rafiq didn't shout. He stood at the whiteboard for a long time, rubbing out and redrawing arrows. Then he called two of us over. "The payment screens and the testing now decide our end date. Leela, you and Varsha move there, today." He moved the dark-mode feature and the new icons into a column marked "after launch". Some people grumbled. By Friday the payment work was two days ahead of the new plan. Rafiq's jaw looked tight all week, but he kept saying, "We'll make it."

qa.q: What did Rafiq move to the 'after launch' column?
qa.a: The dark-mode feature and the new icons.

qa.q: What does Rafiq's tight jaw and 'We'll make it' suggest?
qa.a: He seems tense but determined, worried about the date yet set on steering the team through.

qa.q: What else could Rafiq do to keep the team on side?
qa.a: Explain to the grumbling developers why their features wait, and promise a date to pick them up after launch.

qa.q: How might the developers whose features were delayed feel?
qa.a: They may feel disappointed or sidelined, which is why a clear reason and a future date matter.

grounding: When the approval slips, the lead moves two developers onto the tasks that now decide the end date and lets non-critical items wait.

subtype: Approach: redraws the path when a delay appears and shifts resources [Revision]
passage:
Monday: Jagdish's plan looked fine. Store approval by the 10th, launch on the 20th. Shalini was building the loyalty-points screen.

Thursday: The store emailed: approval delayed a week. Jagdish's coffee went cold as he stared at the chart. The payment tests and the final security check now touched the launch date directly. The loyalty screen didn't. He called Shalini and another developer in. "I'm moving you both to security and payment testing from today. Loyalty points can wait till the update." Shalini hesitated. "I'm halfway through." "I know. Save it. It'll be first after launch."

The following Wednesday: Security and payment passed two days early. The launch held on the 20th. Shalini reopened her loyalty screen, smiling slightly.

qa.q: When was the launch planned for?
qa.a: On the 20th.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel when she was moved off the loyalty screen?
qa.a: She felt reluctant and a bit frustrated, being halfway through, though she accepted the reason.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Moving two developers to the tasks that now touched the launch date and letting loyalty wait, so the delay didn't push the launch.

qa.q: What would change if Jagdish had left Shalini on the loyalty screen?
qa.a: Security and payment testing would likely have finished late, pushing the launch past the 20th for a feature that could wait.

grounding: A lead redraws the path after an approval delay, shifts two developers to the critical tasks and lets non-critical items wait.

subtype: Approach: does similar chores together [Action]
passage:
Art teacher's note, Class 4B, Thursday

Today Simran finished her monsoon painting fifteen minutes before the bell. Usually the children rinse one brush, close one colour, then open another, and the table stays messy until the end. Simran did it differently. She lined up all six brushes and washed them together in the big jar, then laid them flat on newspaper. Then she capped every paint tube at once and stacked the palettes. Her table was clear in five minutes. Himani, beside her, watched and copied. I asked Simran why. She said, "If I do it one by one, I keep stopping, and I forget some." I've asked her to show the class next week.

qa.q: How many brushes did Simran wash together?
qa.a: All six brushes.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt when the teacher asked her to show the class?
qa.a: She was probably proud and a bit shy, pleased her way was noticed.

qa.q: How could the teacher help the whole class tidy this way?
qa.a: Set out one big jar and one tray, then ask everyone to wash all brushes and cap all paints at the end, not after each colour.

qa.q: How does Himani see Simran's way of tidying?
qa.a: Himani seems curious and impressed, so she copies it.

grounding: A girl washes all her brushes and puts all colours away at once after painting, instead of tidying after each colour.

subtype: Approach: does similar chores together [Action]
passage:
Saturday

I made Nani's birthday card today with my watercolours. Last time I painted, I washed my brush after every colour and closed each little pan, and it took forever and Mummy said, "Ritu beti, the sink looks like a rainbow!". So today I tried a new way. I painted everything first. Then I put ALL the brushes in one cup of water and washed them together. Then I closed the whole paint box in one go and put the rag and cup away. Done in five minutes! Sunaina, my little sister, asked why I didn't wash in between. I said, "Because stopping again and again is boring and I forget things." The card has a peacock on it 🦚 Nani will love it.

qa.q: What did Ritu paint on the card?
qa.a: A peacock, on Nani's birthday card.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel about the new way of tidying?
qa.a: Ritu felt pleased and a bit proud, finishing in five minutes instead of forever.

qa.q: What else could Ritu batch next time she paints?
qa.a: Ritu could set out water, rag and all colours before starting, so she doesn't get up again and again.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina see it differently?
qa.a: Sunaina is little and may think washing in between is the right way, because that's what she has seen before.

grounding: A girl washes all her brushes and closes all her colours at once after painting instead of after each colour.

subtype: Approach: groups similar homework into one session [Action]
passage: I'm Anirban, Class 10, and my homework used to take forever. I'd do half a history reading, then an English essay paragraph, then back to history, then a geography question. My sister Vasudha timed me one evening and said, "You spent twenty minutes just opening and closing books." That stung, but she was right. So I tried something. First, all the reading: history chapter, geography pages, the English story. Pencil notes in the margins, nothing else. Then all the writing: essay, answers, summary, one after another. The first night I still wanted to jump around. By the second week, I was done by eight instead of ten. It's not magic. My head just doesn't have to change gears every ten minutes.

qa.q: By what time was Anirban finishing homework by the second week?
qa.a: By eight instead of ten.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel when Vasudha timed the homework?
qa.a: It stung; Anirban felt a bit embarrassed but agreed she was right.

qa.q: What could Anirban try if one subject's reading is very long?
qa.a: Split it into two reading blocks, still keeping reading and writing apart, with a short break between.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see the change?
qa.a: Vasudha would likely feel pleased her timing made a difference, and maybe get more of Anirban's company in the evenings.

grounding: A student groups all reading tasks and then all writing tasks, finding that switching often wastes time and focus.

subtype: Approach: groups similar homework into one session [Action]
passage: I'm Varun, Kishore's younger brother, and we share a desk. Kishore used to have six books open at once, jumping from maths to Hindi to science, sighing a lot. This year I saw him change. He'd put a sticky note on the wall: READ, then WRITE. From six to seven he only read, his history and science chapters, lips moving, pencil marks in the margins. Then he'd stretch, drink water and, from seven, only write: his Hindi essay, then science answers, then history. His pile of open books got smaller. One night I asked why. He shrugged. "Changing subjects every ten minutes eats my brain." I don't know if it works for everyone, but he's been finishing before dinner.

qa.q: What did Kishore's sticky note say?
qa.a: READ, then WRITE.

qa.q: What did Kishore's sighing over six open books suggest?
qa.a: He seemed frustrated and tired, feeling scattered by jumping between subjects.

qa.q: What else could Kishore do to keep his focus?
qa.a: Keep his phone in another room during each block, so the only switch is the planned one at seven.

qa.q: How might Varun be affected by Kishore's new routine?
qa.a: Varun gets a calmer, tidier shared desk and sees an example he might try himself.

grounding: An observer sees a teenager group reading tasks together and writing tasks together to stop wasting time switching.

subtype: Approach: batches errands into one trip [Thinking]
passage: So I'm Lavanya, and in my first year at the hill college, I kept going down to town three times a week. The bus takes forty minutes each way. One Monday it was stationery, Wednesday the laundry, Friday the bank to update my passbook. My roommate Rehana laughed. "You're spending four hours a week on buses." I sat with my notebook and thought it through. The bank opens at ten. The laundry takes a whole day. The stationery shop is next to the bus stop. So: drop laundry first, straight to the bank when it opens, stationery on the way back, pick up laundry the next trip. Now it's one trip on Saturday, and I use the other evenings to study. Rehana calls it my errand train.

qa.q: How long does the bus to town take each way?
qa.a: Forty minutes each way.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when Rehana laughed about the buses?
qa.a: Lavanya felt a little silly, but it pushed some careful thinking about the trips.

qa.q: What else could Lavanya add to the Saturday trip?
qa.a: Anything else from town Lavanya needs that week, like medicines or a phone recharge, written on the same list before leaving.

qa.q: How does Rehana see Lavanya's new routine?
qa.a: Rehana seems amused and approving, giving it a fond nickname, the errand train.

grounding: A hostel student works out how to combine stationery, laundry and the bank into one trip to town instead of three.

subtype: Approach: batches errands into one trip [Thinking]
passage: I'm Simran, and I live next door to Tarun in the college hostel. Every week I'd see Tarun leaving on his cycle, once for printouts and pens, once with a laundry bag, and once to the bank. One Sunday he sat on the steps with a pencil, scribbling a list and muttering. "Laundry takes a day. Bank shuts at two on Saturdays. Stationery's opposite the bank." The next Saturday he left at ten with the laundry bag on his carrier and a folded list in his pocket. He was back by one, with a new pen tucked behind his ear. He went back the next Saturday for the laundry, and picked up printouts on the way. I don't know if he planned it or just got lazy, but he seemed happier.

qa.q: When does the bank shut on Saturdays?
qa.a: At two on Saturdays.

qa.q: What might Tarun be feeling when he came back by one?
qa.a: He seemed relaxed and happier, maybe pleased that one trip did the job of three.

qa.q: What small step could help Tarun make it even smoother?
qa.a: Keep the list on his door all week and add items as he runs out, so nothing is forgotten on Saturday.

qa.q: How might Simran be affected by watching Tarun's new habit?
qa.a: Simran is curious and might start batching errands too, having seen it free up his week.

grounding: An observer watches a hostel student reason about stationery, laundry and the bank and combine them into one trip.

subtype: Approach: batches emails in fixed slots to protect deep work [Action]
passage:
Team lead's note on Uday, month two

Uday joined us as a junior developer and at first answered every message the moment it arrived. His code reviews were full of small slips. Last week he came to me with a plan. He would check chat and email only at eleven and at four, keep the morning from nine to eleven for coding with notifications off, and put a status note up: "Coding till 11, message again if urgent." Bhupen, who sits next to him, was sceptical. This week Uday finished the search feature two days early, and his review had one comment instead of eleven. I've asked him to share his routine at Friday's stand-up.

qa.q: At what times does Uday check messages?
qa.a: At eleven and at four.

qa.q: What might Uday have been feeling when he came with the plan?
qa.a: He probably felt frustrated with his slips and hopeful that protecting his mornings would help.

qa.q: What could Uday add so urgent issues aren't missed?
qa.a: Keep the status note that invites a second message if urgent, or give the team lead a way to call during coding time.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Uday's routine now?
qa.a: Bhupen was sceptical at first, but after the early search feature he may be impressed and curious to try it.

grounding: A developer checks messages at fixed times and keeps the morning free for coding, so he is not interrupted all day.

subtype: Approach: batches emails in fixed slots to protect deep work [Action]
passage:
Tuesday

Day four of the new rule and I actually wrote code this morning. Real code, two hours of it. Until last week I'd be halfway through a function and the chat would ping, and I'd answer, and then spend ten minutes finding where I was. Omkar said I looked like a startled pigeon every time my phone buzzed. So now: notifications off from nine. I check messages at eleven and at four, and I answer everything in one go. I put a line in my status, "Deep work till 11, call if on fire." Nobody called. Today I finished the login fix before lunch. At eleven there were fourteen messages. Not one was urgent. Honestly, that's the biggest surprise. I'm Raghav and I have been a pigeon too long.

qa.q: How many messages were waiting at eleven?
qa.a: Fourteen messages.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel about what the fourteen messages turned out to be?
qa.a: That not one of the fourteen messages was urgent; Raghav felt relieved and a bit amused by it.

qa.q: What else could Raghav try to keep this working?
qa.a: Tell the team the two check times so they know when to expect replies, and keep the call-if-on-fire line.

qa.q: How might Omkar see the change?
qa.a: Omkar probably finds it funny and good, seeing Raghav calmer and no longer jumping at every buzz.

grounding: A developer checks messages at fixed times and keeps the morning free for coding to avoid constant interruptions.

subtype: Approach: batches so long that urgent matters wait too long [Pitfall]
passage: At the travel agency office, Keerthana had made a rule after reading about focus: she read and replied to chats just once daily, at six in the evening. Her mornings were for planning tours. At 10:15 on Wednesday, Baljeet, a junior, messaged her: "Client's flight cancelled. They land in Kochi tonight with no hotel. Can I book the backup at the higher rate?" Keerthana didn't see it. Baljeet waited, then sent another. Then he walked to her cabin, but the door was shut with a "Focus time" sign, and he didn't dare knock. At six she read it. By then the backup hotel was full, and the client had spent hours at the airport. Baljeet sat at his desk, face grey.

qa.q: At what time did Baljeet send the first message?
qa.a: At 10:15 on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when he stood at the shut cabin door?
qa.a: He was anxious and stuck, afraid to knock on the focus-time door while the client waited.

qa.q: What would you change first about Keerthana's rule?
qa.a: Keep focus time but set a clear way to reach her for urgent client issues, like a call or a knock rule.

qa.q: How did the client experience the delay?
qa.a: The client spent hours at the airport with no hotel, likely feeling stranded and let down.

grounding: A manager answers messages only once a day, so a colleague's urgent question about a client sits unanswered until evening.

subtype: Approach: batches so long that urgent matters wait too long [Pitfall]
passage:
Subject: About yesterday

Dear Mridul,

I owe you an apology. Yesterday at 11 a.m. you messaged me that the client's payment had bounced and asked whether to hold their shipment. I only saw it at 7 p.m., because I've been answering messages once a day to protect my focus time. By then the truck had left, and we now have to recover goods from a client who hasn't paid. That isn't your fault. You did the right thing by asking. I made it too hard for you to reach me.

From today I'll check messages three times a day, and if something is urgent, please call me directly, even if my status says busy. I'd rather be interrupted than leave you stuck like that again.

Preeti

qa.q: When did Preeti see Mridul's message?
qa.a: Preeti only saw it at 7 p.m.

qa.q: How does Preeti seem to feel, writing the email?
qa.a: Preeti feels regretful and responsible, apologising and saying it isn't Mridul's fault.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Preeti's team better?
qa.a: Checking messages a few times a day with a direct call for urgent matters keeps focus without leaving people stuck.

qa.q: What was it like for Mridul to wait all day?
qa.a: Mridul was probably anxious and stuck, knowing the shipment question was urgent but unable to get an answer.

grounding: A manager answering messages once a day leaves a colleague's urgent client question unanswered until evening.
